title: Modern view of activated rate processes: unidirectional fluxes at equilibrium, correlation functions, and splitting probabilities
authors: Alexander M. Berezhkovskii, Kevin Song, Dmitrii E. Makarov
abstract: More than 80 years ago Kramers published a paper calculating how fast a Brownian particle escapes from a potential well over an activation barrier. Since then Kramers' model has been widely adopted by nuclear physics, biophysics and chemical physics communities as a description of activated barrier crossing. From a chemical kinetics perspective, Kramers' theory provides a mapping from continuous dynamics to discrete-state chemical kinetics. Motivated by recent developments, this Perspective provides a rigorous way of performing such a mapping, explaining why and how Kramers' theory works from several points of view. Specifically, we consider transitions of a Brownian particle between two potential wells corresponding to the ``reactant'' and the ``product'' of a chemical reaction. A central unifying idea is to divide the equilibrium ensemble of possible states of the system into two sub-ensembles corresponding to the reactant and product states and then to consider fluxes between these sub-ensembles. Importantly, naive separation based on the location measured relative to the barrier top does not result in a mapping that is physically tenable, and instead the past of the trajectory should be considered. Thus constructed reactant and product ensembles provide an internally consistent description of the problem when also viewed from two different perspectives: one based on the definition of the rate as a conditional transition probability per unit time and the other based on the relaxation modes of the time-evolution operator governing the dynamics.
summary: This perspective paper rigorously re-derives the theory of activated rate processes, showing how continuous Brownian motion maps onto discrete chemical kinetics. It resolves ambiguities in defining reaction rates by introducing a concept of unidirectional flux based on trajectory history rather than simple spatial partitioning. This provides a unified and robust theoretical tool for studying barrier crossing phenomena.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a rigorous theoretical framework for mapping continuous, diffusive dynamics (like Brownian motion) onto discrete-state chemical kinetics describing activated barrier crossing.
main_result: It establishes that the rate constant can be calculated robustly by considering unidirectional fluxes between sub-ensembles defined by trajectory history, yielding results consistent with established theories like Kramers' theory and correlation function methods.
method: The authors use concepts from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, analyzing fluxes in phase space and comparing different mathematical formulations (e.g., conditional probabilities vs. relaxation modes) to ensure physical consistency.
model_or_system: The model is a particle undergoing Brownian motion between two potential wells ('reactant' and 'product') separated by an activation barrier $U(x)$. The dynamics are governed by the Langevin or Smoluchowski equation.
key_observables: Reaction rate coefficients ($k_{A	o B}$), equilibrium populations, and the unidirectional reactive flux ($J_{A 	o B}$).
important_parameters: The barrier height relative to thermal energy ($U(0) - U(a) \gg k_BT$) is a crucial parameter for simplifying assumptions.
main_assumptions: Naive state separation based only on position fails; the analysis requires considering the full trajectory history and assuming high barriers allow flux independence from boundary placement.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates two methods of mapping continuous dynamics to discrete states (position cut vs. trajectory history). Figure 2 conceptually shows the cycle of ensemble members leading to a net unidirectional flux.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by reviewing Kramers' theory, identifying the mathematical shortcomings of simple state separation, and then rigorously constructing an internally consistent mapping using fluxes derived from both conditional probabilities and time-evolution operator analysis.
why_interesting: This work provides advanced theoretical tools for calculating rates in complex systems where dynamics are governed by free energy landscapes, which is foundational knowledge for understanding relaxation processes in many quantum or mesoscopic physical systems.
